# Volume 2 — XXX A Wedding at the Stone House

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The final week of August arrived. It was the period set for Miss Rosalind's wedding. Nell and Hugh were departing for Wexcombe College two weeks after that. Within a week, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby planned to relocate to Grey Shutters and establish her lares and penates inside the former spare room, a space that was prepared for her arrival already. Having disposed of every bit of her excess household furniture through an auction, she was currently delighting in the agreeable task of assisting the Waces with their packing. The following Sunday was when Mr. Wace was scheduled to deliver his final sermon. As Nell perceived with a faint sorrow woven through all of her anticipation and joy, the old order was swiftly transforming to make way for the new.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0000 }

“Modifications are not entirely agreeable, yet they are wonderful affairs,” Mr. Pettifer remarked with philosophy. “A couple of years is roughly sufficient time for circumstances to remain completely unchanged. Should they remain stationary for any greater duration, they could become covered in moss.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0001 }

Mr. Pettifer engaged in smoking upon his veranda. A willingness had been expressed by his wife, out of self-sacrifice, allowing him to smoke within the house provided he was attentive to sit near an open window. Mr. Pettifer repaid this compromise by stepping outside entirely for his smoking during pleasant weather, thereby maintaining a spirit of mutual goodwill.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0002 }

Nell had arrived to request a few of her yellow dahlias from Mrs. Pettifer. That night, she and Isolde were heading to Echo Cottage so they could assist Miss Rosalind and Belinda the Fourth in making their last preparations for the wedding the next day. Miss Rosalind herself did not ever keep dahlias; she disliked them, nor would they have fitted the refined seclusion of her old-style garden. However, owing to Uncle Zeb’s storm, blooms of any sort were somewhat rare that summer in Brierley and the surrounding areas; thus Nell and Isolde believed a particular old cream-colored stone jug, which was normally reserved for doughnuts, filled to the top with yellow dahlias, would serve perfectly placed in a dark corner of the stone house staircase, set against the deep backdrop of red wallpaper in the hall.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0003 }

“I guess you’ll be leaving for college in two weeks?” Mr. Pettifer went on. “Indeed, Emily and I are going to miss you terribly. Of course, Mrs. Sowerby will be across there instead of you. Nobody except a replacement can be found for those people.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0004 }

Paper cannot convey the sheer irony that marked Mr. Pettifer’s tone. Regardless of how close his wife was to Mrs. Sowerby, an armed neutrality remained the highest standard achievable for the connection between her and Mr. Pettifer, even after the new regime began.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0005 }

“Indeed, I am leaving,” Nell remarked. “My mind feels quite pleased . . . while my heart feels deeply saddened.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0006 }

“I guess you will be gathering every single honor that happens to be available at Wexcombe.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0007 }

“I might attempt to win a couple of those,” Nell admitted, “however, such achievements hold less value for me than they did a pair of years in the past. My objective for my time at college is acquiring an understanding of how to live in the finest manner and make the absolute most of it. My desire is to gain the ability to comprehend and assist both myself and others.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0008 }

Mr. Pettifer nodded.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0009 }

“Precisely so. Colleges should exist for that purpose, rather than for producing numerous B.A.‘s who are so packed with academic knowledge and self-conceit that nothing else can fit inside them. You are fine. I suppose college will not manage to damage you very much.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0010 }

Following tea, Isolde and Nell traveled to Echo Cottage, bringing along every bit of floral plunder acquired from a series of raiding trips through their own and nearby gardens. Upon arrival, they discovered that the stone residence was buzzing with activity. Belinda the Fourth was darting about with immense energy and speed, making her blue bows appear capable of existing in all places simultaneously. Much like the helmet of Navarre, the blue bows belonging to Belinda fluttered perpetually in the midst of the wildest commotion.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0011 }

“Thank goodness you arrived,” she remarked piously, “since a multitude of chores remains . . . and the icing on that cake refuses to set . . . and every bit of silver still requires polishing . . . and the horsehair trunk needs packing . . . and the roosters destined for the chicken salad are still strutting past the henhouse over there, crowing, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. Moreover, Miss Rosalind cannot be relied upon to perform a single task. I felt relieved when Mr. Stanhope arrived a short while back and escorted her away for a stroll through the forest. Romance is fine where it belongs, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, but combining it with culinary work and cleaning ruins the whole affair. That is how I see it, Miss Harcourt, ma’am.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0012 }

So diligently did Nell and Isolde labor that Belinda the Fourth found nothing to complain about by the time ten o’clock arrived. Plaiting her hair into countless braids, she retired to bed with her exhausted small frame.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0013 }

“However, I am certain I will not sleep a single moment, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, because I am afraid that an issue will arise right at the end . . . the cream will fail to whip . . . or Mr. Stanhope will suffer a stroke, preventing him from attending.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0014 }

“Is he accustomed to suffering strokes?” inquired Isolde, as the dimpled edges of her mouth quivered. In the eyes of Isolde, Belinda the Fourth was a perpetual joy, even if she was not precisely a beautiful sight.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0015 }

“These are not events that follow routine,” Belinda the Fourth stated with composure. “They simply occur . . . and then it is done. A stroke can happen to anyone. It does not require practice. Mr. Stanhope bears a strong resemblance to a relative of mine who suffered one right as he was sitting down to eat dinner a while back. However, perhaps things will turn out fine. While living in this world, a person must merely wish for the best, get ready for the worst, and accept whatever comes from God.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0016 }

“My sole concern is that the weather will not be good tomorrow,” Isolde stated. “Rain was forecasted for midweek by Uncle Zeb, and I have been unable to avoid thinking Uncle Zeb’s words carry significant weight ever since that major storm.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0017 }

Because Nell understood far more clearly than Isolde the precise extent of Uncle Zeb's involvement in the tempest, this did not cause her much distress. She enjoyed the deep slumber reserved for those who are righteous and exhausted, until Belinda the Fourth awakened her at a extraordinarily early hour.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0018 }

“Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, it’s awful to call you so early,” wailed through the keyhole, “but there’s so much to do yet . . . and oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, I’m skeered it’s going to rain and I wish you’d get up and tell me you think it ain’t.” Hoping desperately that Belinda the Fourth uttered this just to wake her up completely, Nell rushed over to the window. However, the morning appeared dismal, unfortunately. Miss Rosalind’s garden below her window was dark and still when it ought to have shone with bright early daylight; furthermore, sullen clouds darkened the sky above the fir trees.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0019 }

“Is it not excessively unkind!” Isolde remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0020 }

“Our hope must be for the best outcome,” Nell said with determination. “Provided it refrains from genuinely raining, an overcast, cool, pearly gray day such as this one will actually prove more pleasant than scorching sun.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0021 }

“Yet rain is coming,” grieved Belinda, entering the room stealthily, looking absurd with her head encircled by numerous plaits whose tips, bound with white cotton, projected every which way. “Rain will be delayed until the ultimate second and then fall in torrents. Subsequently, everyone will become drenched . . . and bring mud into every corner of the dwelling . . . and holding the wedding beneath the honeysuckle will be impossible . . . and a bride deprived of sunshine suffers terrible misfortune, whatever you might claim, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. My intuition warned me that our good fortune was too great to endure.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0022 }

Belinda the Fourth appeared without doubt to have taken a page from the book of Miss Eliza Pullen.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0023 }

Precipitation never fell, even if the sky continually appeared ready to deliver it. The chambers had been embellished and the table exquisitely arranged when midday arrived; meanwhile on the upper floor, a bride was expecting her groom, “adorned for her husband.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0024 }

“You really do appear sweet,” Nell remarked enthusiastically.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0025 }

“Lovely,” Isolde repeated.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0026 }

“Everything’s ready, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, and nothing dreadful has happened yet,” declared a cheerful Belinda before she went into her small back room to get dressed. Undoing all her braids, she took the wild crinkles that remained, plaited them into two pigtails, and fastened them using four brand-new, vivid blue ribbon bows instead of just two. Sprouting from Belinda’s neck, the pair of top bows looked remarkably like oversized wings, much like those on Raphael’s cherubs. Nevertheless, they were considered extremely lovely by Belinda the Fourth, who, having rustled into a white dress starched so heavily it was capable of standing on its own, looked at her reflection in the mirror with immense pride . . . a pride that endured right up to the moment she stepped into the hallway and saw, through the open spare room door, a tall girl wearing a softly draped dress, who was placing white, star-like blossoms into the sleek waves of her reddish hair.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0027 }

“Oh, I shall not ever manage to resemble Miss Harcourt,” poor Belinda reflected in desperation. “A person simply must be created that way, I suppose . . . it does not appear as though any degree of training could grant a person that carriage.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0028 }

The visitors had arrived by one o’clock, among them Mr. and Mrs. Wace, because Mr. Wace was scheduled to conduct the service while the Welby minister was away on vacation. The wedding lacked any ceremony. Miss Rosalind descended the steps to join her groom at the bottom, and when he grabbed her hand she raised her large brown eyes to his with an expression that caused Belinda the Fourth, who caught the glance, to feel more peculiar than before. They walked outside to the honeysuckle arbor, the place where Mr. Wace was expecting them. The visitors arranged themselves in whatever manner they preferred. Nell and Isolde stood near the ancient stone bench, having Belinda the Fourth positioned between them while she frantically held onto their hands with her icy, shaking small paws.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0029 }

When Mr. Wace unclasped his blue book, the ritual began. At the exact moment that Miss Rosalind and Stephen Stanhope were declared husband and wife, an exceptionally lovely and meaningful event occurred. Without warning, the sun broke past the gloom and showered an abundance of light upon the joyful bride. Immediately, the garden became filled with moving shadows and shimmering rays.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0030 }

“What a lovely omen,” Nell thought while she hurried over to kiss the bride. Afterwards, leaving the remaining guests behind as they laughed around the newlyweds, the three girls sped inside the house to ensure that everything was prepared for the feast.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0031 }

“Thank goodness that it has finished, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” Belinda the Fourth gasped, “and no matter what takes place from this point on, they are wedded safe and sound. Ma’am, the rice bags can be found in the pantry, the worn shoes sit behind the door, and the whipping cream has been placed on the sullar steps.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0032 }

When it reached 2:30, Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope departed, whereupon all the people traveled to Alder River so that they might bid them farewell on the train running in the afternoon. When Miss Rosalind . . . I ask her forgiveness, Mrs. Stanhope . . . walked out through the doorway belonging to the house of her youth, Hugh along with the girls cast the rice, while an old shoe was flung by Belinda the Fourth using such great accuracy that Mr. Wace was hit directly upon his head. It was Cedric, however, who held the role of providing the most charming farewell. He emerged suddenly from the porch while vigorously ringing a massive ancient brass dinner bell that had decorated the mantel in the dining room. Making a happy sound served as the sole intention of Cedric; yet when the loud noise faded, there echoed from the point, the bend, and the hill on the opposite side of the river the peeling of “fairy wedding bells,” which rang out in a clear, sweet, and increasingly faint manner, precisely as though the cherished echoes of Miss Rosalind were offering her a welcome and a goodbye. Thus, surrounded by this blessing composed of lovely noises, Miss Rosalind departed by carriage from her former existence filled with dreams and pretenses toward a richer existence of truths inside the active world outside.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0033 }

A pair of hours afterward, Nell alongside Belinda the Fourth walked down the lane once more. Since Hugh had departed for West Welby to run a chore and Isolde was required to attend a home commitment, Nell and Belinda returned for the purpose of tidying up and securing the small stone dwelling. Late, golden sunlight flooded the garden, where bees hummed and butterflies fluttered; nevertheless, the small house held that elusive sense of gloom that invariably succeeds a celebration.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0034 }

“My goodness, doesn't it seem deserted?” sobbed Belinda the Fourth, who had not stopped weeping throughout the entire trip back from the station. “When everything is finished, Miss Harcourt, ma'am, a wedding isn't really much happier than a funeral.”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0035 }

An active night came next. It was necessary to take down the decorations, clean the dishes, and store the leftover treats in a basket to delight Belinda the Fourth’s younger brothers at their house. Nell refused to take a break before every last thing was in perfect condition; once Belinda had departed for home bearing her loot, Nell walked through the quiet rooms, experiencing the sensation of somebody stepping by themselves in an abandoned banquet hall, and pulled the blinds shut. Next, she secured the door with a key and took a seat beneath the silver poplar so she could await Hugh, experiencing great fatigue yet continuing to ponder “long, long thoughts” without growing weary.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0036 }

“Nell, what is on your mind?” inquired Hugh, as he walked down the path. Outside by the road, he had left his buggy and horse.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0037 }

“About Miss Rosalind and Mr. Stanhope,” Nell replied in a dreamy manner. “Is it not wonderful to consider the way all things have resolved . . . the manner in which they are reunited at last following every year of distance and misapprehension?”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0038 }

“Indeed, it is lovely,” stated Hugh, gazing intently down at the raised face of Nell, “yet would it not have been even finer, Nell, had no rift or misapprehension ever occurred . . . had they traveled side by side through their entire existence, possessing no recollections from the past except the ones they shared together?”
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0039 }

Nell’s heart beat strangely for an instant, her eyes wavering beneath Hugh’s look for the very first time as a pink blush colored her pale face. A curtain suspended before her internal awareness seemed to rise, exposing hidden emotions and truths to her sight. Maybe romance failed to arrive in a person's existence with fanfare and pageantry, resembling a splendid knight riding forth; maybe it slipped to a person's flank through peaceful paths like an ancient companion; maybe it manifested as ordinary writing, right up until an abrupt beam of light cast across the sheets revealed the cadence and the melody, maybe . . . maybe . . . love blossomed effortlessly from a lovely companionship, just as a yellow-centered rose emerges from its calyx.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0040 }

Afterwards the curtain fell once more; yet the Nell who trod the gloomy avenue was not entirely the identical Nell who had ridden merrily along it the previous night. An invisible hand had flipped the leaf of girlhood, leaving the leaf of womanhood lying open in front of her, complete with its fascination and secrecy, its suffering and joy.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0041 }

Hugh prudently refrained from further speech; nevertheless, within his quietude, he foresaw the events of the subsequent four years through the memory of Nell’s rosy cheeks. Four years filled with dedicated, joyful labor . . . followed ultimately by the reward of practical wisdom acquired and a tender heart secured.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0042 }

In the garden behind them, the small house of stone brooded amidst the shadows. Though lonely, it was not abandoned. Dreams, laughter, and the zest for life were not yet finished with it; upcoming summers awaited the small house of stone; for now, it was able to wait. And across the river, held in purple captivity, the echoes awaited their moment.
{: #nw-v02-c30-p0043 }
